overview: Tokugawa Ieyasu founded a hereditary military government in 1603. From Edo, now Tokyo, its shoguns governed alongside regional lords called daimyo. Their long rule supported expanding towns, commerce and learning, while preserving strong inequalities. This map displays only 1650 to 1783; the shogunate continued until 1868. The broad northern coloring obscures Ainu lands and changing frontier relationships, not uniform control. Earlier and later examples below are dated separately.

periods.title: Building the shogunal order
periods.summary: The Tokugawa established hereditary authority over a network of regional domains.

periods.title: Established government and controlled exchange
periods.summary: Regional lords remained under shogunal authority; regulated Dutch trade continued at Deshima.

periods.title: Selective opening to foreign knowledge
periods.summary: Yoshimune relaxed restrictions on non-Christian foreign books, encouraging practical learning.

periods.title: The later shogunate
periods.summary: Dutch studies grew through families, schools and an official translation bureau established in 1811.

periods.title: Foreign pressure and political crisis
periods.summary: Perry’s arrival and new treaty negotiations challenged the established system.

sections.title: Power, law and the northern frontier

items.text: The shogun did not personally administer every village. Daimyo governed domains, but the shogunate could relocate them, change their lands or confiscate their holdings. Samurai increasingly staffed offices and managed administration. A hereditary warrior could spend much more time on records and accounts than on a battlefield.

Under alternate attendance, regional lords had to spend set periods in Edo as well as in their domains. Their movements helped the shogunate restrain rivals. Edo was the center of military government, while the imperial court remained in Kyoto: Japan had more than one important center of authority.

The 1615 Laws of Military Households regulated more than fighting. They required study alongside military training, restricted castle construction and demanded approval for marriages among the ruling military households. Family alliances could reshape politics, so choosing a spouse was not simply a private matter for these elites.

The northern map needs particular care. Matsumae received a monopoly on trade with the Ainu in 1604; Shakushain led major resistance in 1669. Direct shogunal government expanded into eastern Ezo only in 1799. Trade monopolies, resistance and later administrative takeovers were different relationships, which one map color cannot distinguish.

Restricted foreign relations still brought goods and knowledge. The Dutch trading station moved to Deshima at Nagasaki in 1641. Interpreters made trade possible; imports included sugar and medicines, while copper, ceramics and lacquerware went abroad. The small trading compound included cooks, carpenters and physicians, as well as merchants.

sections.title: Homes, water and the useful contents of a toilet

items.text: Many ordinary Edo residents rented small units in nagaya row houses. The museum’s reconstruction shows a cooking hearth and water jar beside a dirt-floored entrance, with clothes and bedding stored in boxes or cloth bundles. Thin partitions and combustible materials made close neighbors and fire danger part of daily life.

The Tamagawa waterworks began supplying Edo in 1654. An open channel carried water about forty-three kilometers from Hamura to Yotsuya; wooden and stone conduits continued underground into the city. Surveyors used the land’s gentle fall to move water. Getting the slope right was a very practical achievement.

Toilet waste could have a buyer. Farmers collected stored human waste from townspeople, paying money or exchanging vegetables, then used it as fertilizer. Food traveled into town and nutrients traveled back to fields. This was resource recycling with a distinctly smelly cargo, rather than a modern flush-and-forget sewer system.

Edo’s time bells were a shared service. Records of the Hongokucho bell describe a monthly fee of four mon from people living within earshot, funding the bell’s operation. Your neighborhood could hear the time together; the person ringing it still needed to be paid.

A school board game printed between 1843 and 1847 shows a mother taking a boy to a terakoya, a school teaching reading and writing. Other squares depict practice, rewards and punishments. Its finish is Kameido Tenjin, a shrine associated with learning. Even a game could turn schoolwork into an adventure.

Students practiced with oraimono, books of model letters and sentences. Lessons could differ by occupation, gender and status: merchants, farmers and carpenters had different practical examples. Learning to write might mean preparing for a particular household business or trade, rather than following one identical national curriculum.

Under Yoshimune, government agents searched for medicinal plants and taught local people about useful species. Uemura Masakatsu’s records describe herb-gathering journeys from 1720 to 1753, involving roughly 140 to 190 travel days a year. Studying nature could mean a remarkable amount of walking and careful recording.

In 1720, Yoshimune relaxed the ban on importing non-Christian foreign books. Dutch studies eventually embraced medicine, astronomy and other practical fields. Knowledge also passed through families: the Sugita, Katsuragawa and Udagawa households transmitted this learning between generations, connecting scholarship with family work.

The 1774 Kaitai Shinsho brought a Dutch-derived anatomical work into Japanese scholarship. Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryotaku and collaborators translated it; Odano Naotake supplied illustrations. Four text volumes accompanied a volume of pictures. Medical publishing joined language skills, image making and knowledge of the body in one demanding project.

解體新書, Kaitai shinsho, means “New Book of Anatomy.” These four characters reproduce the title catalogued on a surviving 1774 medical book, using the older form 體 for “body.” The sample is a scholarly transcription of an attested title, not an invented sentence or a copy of someone’s handwriting.

In 1765, richly colored woodblock calendars helped launch nishiki-e, or brocade pictures. Wealthy patrons commissioned calendars to exchange at New Year. A useful object could become a fashionable artwork: before checking the date on a screen, some Edo collectors could check it on an elaborate print.

A woodblock print required a team. A designer prepared the image, a specialist cut the blocks, a printer applied color and printed the sheets, and a publisher organized the venture. Famous artists depended on other craftspeople’s precision. The person whose name we remember was not the only person who made the picture.

Another late-Edo board game takes players through famous places to eat, starting at Nihonbashi’s morning market and ending at the Sanno Festival. Eel and buckwheat noodles appear among its specialties. The start square makes a pun on a bargain sale: food advertising and wordplay were comfortable companions.

Later Edo kabuki could offer ghostly special effects. In The Ghost Story of Yotsuya, backstage devices made a ghost emerge from a lantern or disappear through a wall. The Edo-Tokyo Museum explains the stage machinery behind these surprises. Frightening an audience took skilled teamwork behind the scenes.

ending.text: The 1783 map endpoint was not the shogunate’s fall. Yoshinobu returned political authority to the emperor in 1867 but failed to preserve Tokugawa power. The new Meiji government emerged in 1868. This ended the shogunal system, not Japanese society: people, businesses, scholarship and performing traditions continued through major political change.
